overview.body:
**Nagoya** ​(*nagoya*) — ‌Industrial ‌Hub, ​Chūbu — ​belongs ​to ​the Japanese ​tradition. ‌The ​name means ​"Peaceful ‌ancient house"[^1].

​Nagoya ‌is ​the great ‌industrial ​and ​castle city ​of ​central ​Japan, historically ‌tied ​to the ‌Owari ​Tokugawa ‌house and ​the ‌Atsuta ​Shrine.

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the ​name as ‌**Nagoya**. ‌The plain ‌ASCII ​form ​*nagoya* is ‌the ​modern ​Hepburn romanization; ‌the ​restoration ​capitalizes the ‌conventional ​spelling. Because ‌the ​Japanese ​source script ​uses ​logographic ‌characters whose ‌distinctive ​visual ‌form cannot ​be ​conveyed in ‌the ‌basic ‌Latin alphabet, ‌and ​because ‌no diacritic ​or ​special ​letter is ‌added ​in this ​restoration, ​the ‌name is ​placed ​in ​Tier 2. ‌The ​Unicode ‌form remains ​the ‌philologically complete ​reference, ‌while ‌the ASCII ​spelling ​is ​a practical ​convenience ‌for ‌the domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**名古屋**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Peaceful ancient ​house"[^1].

Nagoya's name ​is traditionally ‌explained as ​"peaceful ancient ​house" (*na-goya*), ‌from *na* ​(peaceful) and ‌*koya/goya* (old house). ​The name ‌first appears ​in the ​*Heike Monogatari* ​and became ​associated with the ​castle town ‌founded by ​Tokugawa Ieyasu ‌in 1610 ​on the ‌site of ​the earlier Oda ‌stronghold. It ​is not ‌a mythic ​deity but ​a place ‌that has ‌acquired sacred and ‌historical resonance.

​The ASCII ​form *nagoya* ‌survives only ​because the ​early domain-name ‌system could not ​carry Japanese ​characters or ‌diacritics; it ​is a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ​**Nagoya** gives ‌the conventional ‌Hepburn romanization ​with initial ‌capitalization, the standard ​scholarly way ​to cite ‌a proper ‌name in ‌romanized Japanese. ‌The name ​is Tier 2 ‌because the ​restoration does ​not add ​a distinctive ‌diacritic or ​special letter ​absent from the ​ASCII form.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **n** ​→ **N** ‌— Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — ​Same
- ‌**g** → ​**g** — ‌Same
- ‌**o** → **o** ​— Same
​- **y** ​→ **y** ​— Same
‌- **a** ‌→ **a** ​— Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/na.ɡo.ja/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'NAGOYA' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Nagoya ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*nagoya* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Nagoya** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Nagoya** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*nagoya* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Nagoya ​is the ‌domain of ‌civic ​identity, industrial ​power, and ​castle ​culture in ​central Japan. ‌As ​the fourth-largest ​city and ‌the ​historic centre ‌of the ​Chūbu ‌region, it ​embodies the ​transition ​from feudal ​castle town ​to ‌modern manufacturing ​capital. Its ‌shrines, ​festivals, and ‌museums preserve ​the ‌memory of ​the Owari ‌Tokugawa ​house.

The ​domain of ‌**Nagoya** ‌is understood ‌within the ​broader ​Japanese religious ‌landscape as ​both ​a specific ‌functional sphere ​and ​a node ‌in a ​network of ‌kami, ​buddhas, and ​local spirits. ​Shrines, ​temples, and ‌household rites ‌all ​invoke the ‌figure in ​ways ​that blur ‌strict boundaries ‌between ‌Shinto and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ​The ‌restoration **Nagoya** ​therefore names ​not ​only a ‌mythic person ​but ​a living ​field of ‌ritual ​activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, iconography, ​and ‌prayer continue ​to define ‌what ​the name ‌means in ​contemporary ‌Japan. This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" ​context is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
Nagoya's ​foundation myth ‌centres on ‌the building ​of Nagoya ​Castle ​in 1610 ​by Tokugawa ​Ieyasu as ‌a bulwark ​against ​Osaka and ‌a residence ​for his ‌son Yoshinao. ​The ‌transfer of ​the *Kusanagi* ​sword to ​Atsuta Shrine ​gave ​the city ‌a sacred ​charge. The ‌*shachi-hoko* ​roof ornaments, ‌gilded to ​impress rivals ‌and to ​ward ‌off fire, ​became the ​visual signature ‌of the ‌castle ‌and the ​city.

The ​narrative of ‌**Nagoya** participates ​in ​the larger ‌mythic program ​of the ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*: to ‌explain the ​origins of ​the imperial ​house, ​the division ‌of divine ‌labour, and ​the relationship ‌between ​the human ​and kami ‌worlds. Because ‌these chronicles ‌were ‌compiled in ​the eighth ‌century under ​imperial patronage, ​the ​myths also ‌serve a ​political theology, ​grounding ​earthly authority ‌in divine ​descent and ​cosmic order[^3]. ​Read ‌comparatively, the ​story of ‌nagoya illustrates ​how Japanese ‌myth ​uses genealogy, ‌descent from ‌heaven, and ​the negotiation ​of ​rival domains ​to construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

sources.citation: Nagoya Castle records and Atsuta Shrine traditions.

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**名古屋** ‌— ​Japanese ​‌logographic ​and ‌syllabic ​script ‌(kanji ​plus ​kana ​where ​attested), ​attested ‌in ​the ‌classical ​Japanese ‌sources. ​The ‌script ​is ‌written ​top-to-bottom ​in ‌‌traditional ‌contexts ​and ​left-to-right ‌in ​modern ​reproductions[^1].

‌The ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌is ​*Nagoya* ‌(Hepburn ​romanization ​with ​initial ​capitalization), ‌giving ‌the ​normalized ‌reading ​​//na.ɡo.ja//.

‌The ‌characters ‌名古屋 ‌are ​semantic: ‌名 ​(name/famous), ​古 ​(old), ‌屋 ​(house). ​They ​are ‌*ateji* ​assigned ​to ​the ‌pre-existing ​place ‌name. ​‌The ​castle ‌名古屋城 ‌(*Nagoya-jō*) ​is ​one ​of ​Japan's ‌most ‌famous ​fortresses.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌do ​not treat ​**Nagoya** primarily ​as ​a mythic ​person but ‌as ​a place ​embedded ‌in the ​sacred geography ‌of ​the Japanese ‌archipelago. The ​chronicles ​map the ​land by ​assigning ​divine origins ‌to its ​mountains, ‌rivers, plains, ​and islands, ‌so ​a site ‌such ​as Nagoya ‌participates in ​this ​cosmogonic project ‌even when ‌it ‌is not ​the protagonist ​of ‌a single ​episode[^1]. Later ​records, ‌including the ​provincial *fudoki*, ​elaborate ‌the local ​kami ‌and traditions ​that grew ​up ​around the ​place.

For ‌scholars, ‌the value ​of the ‌*Kojiki* ​and *Nihon ​Shoki* lies ‌in ‌their preservation ‌of an ‌eighth-century ​vision of ‌the ​land as ​a realm ​charged ‌with kami ​presence. Nagoya ​appears ​within that ‌vision as ​a ​major city ​in central ‌Japan, ​historically a ‌castle town ​of ‌the Owari ​branch ‌of the ‌Tokugawa house, ​a ​status that ​shaped pilgrimage, ​poetry, ‌and political ‌rhetoric for ​centuries[^2].

shinto-sources.body:
The ​Shinto ‌sources for ‌**Nagoya** ​centre ​on ​shrine ​records, ritual ​protocols, ‌and ​the ​priestly ‌traditions that ​maintain ‌the ​site's ‌cult. Shrine ​chronicles ​(*engi*) ​compiled ​from ​the medieval ‌period ​onward ‌recount ​the foundation, ‌miraculous ​origins, ‌and ​patronage ‌of Nagoya, ​while ​liturgical ‌texts ‌preserve ‌the *norito* ​prayers ​offered ‌there[^1]. ​Archaeological and ​architectural ‌evidence ​complements ​these ‌written sources, ​showing ‌how ​the ​site's ​sacred topography ​was ‌developed ‌over ​centuries.

Because ‌Nagoya ​is ​a ‌place, ‌its Shinto ‌identity ‌is ​inseparable ‌from ​the landscape: ​trees, ​springs, ‌rocks, ​and pathways ​all ​function ‌as ​secondary ​scriptures. The ​ritual ‌calendar ​of ‌the shrine—festivals, ​pilgrimages, ‌and ​imperial ‌envoys—provides ‌the living ​context ​in ​which ​the ‌written sources ‌are ​activated[^2].

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
**Nagoya** ​bears ‌a significant ‌Buddhist ​imprint, ​whether ​through ​the presence ​of ‌temples, ​the ​pilgrimage ‌routes that ​traverse ‌the ​site, ‌or the ​medieval ​doctrine ​that ​local ​kami are ‌manifestations ​of ‌Buddhist ​buddhas and ‌bodhisattvas[^1]. ​The ‌*honji-suijaku* ​theory ‌provided the ​theological ​vocabulary ‌for ‌this ‌identification: the ​kami ​of ‌Nagoya ​could be ​understood ‌as ​a ​*suijaku*, ‌or local ​trace, ‌of ​a ​universal ​Buddhist principle.

​After ‌the ‌Meiji ​separation of ‌Shinto ​and ​Buddhism, ‌many ‌Buddhist structures ‌and ‌images ​were ‌removed ​from shrine ​precincts, ​yet ‌the ​artistic, architectural, ​and ​ritual ‌layers ​remain ​visible to ​historians[^2]. ‌Nagoya ​thus ‌preserves a ​palimpsest ‌of ​Japanese ‌religious ‌history, in ​which ​Buddhist ​and ​Shinto ‌claims have ‌alternately ​dominated.

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
